title: Jayaprakash Narayan

cards.b:
Jayaprakash Narayan (JP, 1902-79) travelled from Marxism to Gandhian Sarvodaya and led the movement that challenged Indira Gandhi's rule in the mid-1970s. He gives UPSC three keywords: partyless democracy, Sarvodaya and Total Revolution.

JP led the Bihar Movement from 1974, and the Janata Party won the 1977 general election after the Emergency. He is a key link between student protest and national politics.

In Why Socialism (1936) JP argued for Marxist socialism. By From Socialism to Sarvodaya (1957) he held that state socialism and nationalised industry do not end exploitation and concentrate power. In 1954 he gave up party politics (at Bodh Gaya) to work for Vinoba's Bhoodan.

Sarvodaya means the rise of all, achieved by moral change, not state coercion.

In A Plea for Reconstruction of Indian Polity (1959), JP held that party competition corrupts and centralises. His alternative is a pyramid of village, block, district and state councils, indirectly elected, with candidates chosen by communities and not parties.

It echoes Gandhi's panchayat idea. Critics say it is unworkable, as parties are central to mass democracy.

In the Bihar movement of 1974 (after Gujarat's Nav Nirman agitation), JP called for Sampoorna Kranti at Gandhi Maidan, Patna, on 5 June 1974. It covers seven fields: political, economic, social, cultural, intellectual, educational and spiritual. The idea: change both institutions and people.

Immediate demands: dissolve the Bihar assembly, end corruption, change education.

Following the Allahabad High Court verdict against Indira Gandhi (12 June 1975), JP addressed a rally in Delhi on 25 June. That night, the Emergency was declared and JP was arrested. He was held until November, a failing kidney leading to release. In 1977, he united opposition parties into the Janata Party, which won and ended Congress rule at the Centre.

• His call to the police and army not to obey 'illegal' orders was seen as inviting disorder.
  • The movement was led by students with vague aims.
  • Janata Party's quick collapse (1979) shows the limits of a coalition of opposites.
  • Supporters: he revived mass civic politics and restored democracy.

JP kept Marx's passion for equality and Gandhi's ethical means. He broke with Marx on violence and on the state. Compare Lohia: both came from the socialist left, but Lohia stayed in party politics and focused on caste, while JP moved to a moral, non-party approach.

The 1974 movement pushed the idea of citizen oversight: Lokpal (Anna Hazare's 2011 campaign echoed his anti-corruption theme), right to recall debates, the NOTA right. JP received the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1999. The Bihar leaders Lalu Prasad and Nitish Kumar emerged from his movement.

"What is Total Revolution? Discuss its relevance."
"Examine JP's views on party-based democracy."
"Trace JP's journey from socialism to Sarvodaya."

Structure: journey, Sarvodaya, partyless democracy, Total Revolution, Emergency, critique, relevance.

A strong answer quotes the line from Ramdhari Singh Dinkar's poem used at the 1975 Ramlila Maidan rally: 'Singhasan khali karo ki janata aati hai'.

JP's 1975 call on the police and army not to obey illegal orders, and his demand for a 'Total Revolution', are both quoted in exam answers.
